strengths: Large-scale visual CoT dataset: 489K annotated examples across four domains, plus a 165K VisReason-Pro subset with pseudo-3D/depth-aware annotations, addressing the scarcity of multi-round process-level supervision for MLLMs.

Clear and detailed data-generation pipeline: uses monocular depth, semantic segmentation, iterative global-to-local RoI refinement, single-round distillation, and provides algorithms/prompts in the supplementary material, aiding reproducibility.

Empirical validation: fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B on VisReason/VisReason-Pro improves Visual-CoT benchmark performance and spatial/3D grounding metrics; ablation and human study indicate benefits of the multi-round and adaptive zoom components.

Useful benchmark contribution: introduces evaluation protocols for RoI localization and 3D grounding with metrics such as grounded ratio, BBox IoU, and ordinal depth error, which can support future spatially aware MLLM evaluation.
Well-written and organized: related work, motivation, figures, and implementation details are generally clear, with external evaluations on MME and V* demonstrating generalization.
weaknesses: No human verification of dataset/benchmark annotations: VisReason and VisReason-Pro rationales, RoIs, and pseudo-3D cues are generated by GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini and automatic depth/segmentation models. Claims of 'high-fidelity' or 'expert-level' annotation are not substantiated, and hallucinated or spatially incorrect reasoning may remain.

Circular benchmark ground truth: the VisReason-Pro detection/3D grounding benchmark uses final-round CoT RoI boxes generated by the same automatic pipeline as ground truth. Models are therefore evaluated against another model's outputs, not independent human labels, which can reward annotation-style imitation rather than genuine grounding ability.

Incomplete benchmark evaluation: the new VisReason-Pro benchmark reports only localization and 3D grounding metrics, not final answer accuracy or reasoning faithfulness. Main comparisons are largely on the existing Visual-CoT benchmark, so the proposed benchmark's value for full visual CoT reasoning is not fully demonstrated.

Training/inference protocol mismatch: the model is trained via NLL on serialized multi-step RoI text, while inference/evaluation relies on an explicit tool-call/zoom interface. It is unclear whether the fine-tuned model was trained to emit tool calls, which may affect validity and reproducibility of the reported multi-round results.

Limited experimental scope: only one base model family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) with LoRA is fine-tuned; there are no multiple seeds/significance tests, no comparison to human-annotated CoT data or training on prior visual CoT datasets, and improvements on text/document domains are mixed. The user study is small (30 raters, 20 items).

Incremental novelty relative to prior work: the dataset builds heavily on Visual-CoT and existing source datasets, while global-to-local zoom and depth-aware visual reasoning have precedents in recent MLLM/CoT literature. The contribution is mainly scale and annotation expansion rather than a new problem formulation.

No limitations or broader-impact discussion: potential annotation bias, hallucination propagation, data contamination, licensing/privacy issues, and compute cost are not addressed. This is a notable omission for a large-scale dataset/benchmark paper.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely large-scale visual CoT dataset (489K examples) spanning four diverse domains (text/doc, fine-grained, general VQA, spatial relations), substantially exceeding the scale and domain breadth of prior visual CoT resources such as Visual-CoT, V*, and VPD.

The depth-aware supervision (VisReason-Pro) is a meaningful and relatively novel extension over existing 2D-grounding visual CoT datasets: it uses monocular depth (Depth-Anything V2) and semantic segmentation (Mask2Former/SAM2) to produce pseudo-3D cues and ordinal-depth relations, enabling 'in front of / behind' style reasoning that prior 2D-only datasets lack.

Comprehensive and well-structured evaluation: Visual-CoT-Benchmark (11 source sets), a dedicated VisReason-Pro benchmark (RoI localization + 3D grounding), plus MME and V* generalization, with a clean multi-round zoom evaluation protocol that mirrors training.

Solid empirical results: VisReason-Pro-7B achieves the best open-source average (0.807) on the Visual-CoT-Benchmark and strong results on V* (0.619), with meaningful gains in fine-grained recognition and spatial reasoning over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone.

Ablations (Table 6) and a blinded human study with 30 raters (Table 7) provide additional, multi-faceted evidence for the value of multi-round, depth-aware, zoom-in supervision, going beyond single-metric reporting.

High level of reproducibility detail: complete training hyperparameters, LoRA config, data-generation algorithms (Algorithms 1-2), and all prompts (Figs. 7-15) are provided in the supplementary material.
Clear, well-organized writing with helpful illustrative figures that make the multi-round zoom-and-verify paradigm easy to understand.
weaknesses: The dataset is generated largely by GPT-4.1 / GPT-4.1-nano via prompting; there is no systematic human verification or error-rate analysis of the generated rationales, RoIs, or final justifications. This raises concerns about annotation noise, hallucinated rationales, and teacher-model bias propagating into the 'ground truth' CoT traces.

The '3D grounding' claim rests on pseudo-GT derived from monocular depth estimation (Depth-Anything V2), which is itself approximate. The paper does not analyze how depth-estimation errors affect the ordinal-depth supervision or the evaluation, so the strong '3D-aware reasoning' framing slightly oversells the underlying evidence.

The core 'zoom-and-verify / global-to-local' paradigm is already established in prior work (V*, Chain-of-Focus, Visual-CoT, Pixel Reasoner). The main novel ingredients here are scale, additional domains, and depth cues, so the conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental.

The absolute 3D-grounding numbers are modest (grounded ratio 0.276, IoU 0.278, depth abs error 0.266 in Table 4), and the metric definitions (e.g., matching predicted to ground-truth objects by lowercased text names) are somewhat loose, so the practical significance of the 'depth-aware' advantage is not fully established.

The overall gains from adding VisReason-Pro and adaptive zoom-in are fairly small (e.g., avg 0.770 → 0.791 → 0.807 in Table 6), which makes it difficult to attribute improvements cleanly and raises questions about the marginal value of the depth-informed subset.

Evaluation on the Visual-CoT-Benchmark uses an LLM-as-judge similarity grader, and some baseline numbers are taken from prior papers rather than re-run under the authors' protocol; this introduces potential evaluation inconsistency and judge noise.

The model is still slightly worse than its Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone on text/doc tasks (0.928 vs 0.964), which the paper acknowledges but does not deeply analyze, leaving open whether the depth-aware CoT supervision trades off core perceptual ability.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and timely gap: large-scale, process-level (multi-round) visual CoT supervision with explicit spatial grounding, which existing datasets such as Visual-CoT, VPD, and CoT-Spot only partially address.

The dataset is large (489K examples) and spans four clearly motivated domains (text/doc, fine-grained, general VQA, spatial relation reasoning), with a curated 165K VisReason-Pro subset that adds depth/segmentation-derived cues.

The construction pipeline is documented in unusual detail (Algorithms 1-2, full prompt set in the supplementary), which supports reproducibility of the pipeline design and makes the methodology auditable.

Evaluation is broad: 11 Visual-CoT subsets plus MME and V* for cross-benchmark generalization, a dedicated RoI/3D-grounding benchmark, ablations (Table 6), and a human study (Table 7) that supports gains in grounded faithfulness and stepwise clarity.
The paper is generally clearly written and well organized, and the qualitative examples (Figs. 1, 6, 16-22) effectively illustrate the intended global-to-local, zoom-and-verify behavior.
weaknesses: The CoT annotations are generated with the ground-truth answer provided in the prompt (Algorithm 1: prompt G with (I, q, a); final justification uses (I_final, q, a, B*)). This is post-hoc rationalization rather than reasoning supervision, which is a fundamental concern for a dataset whose central claim is teaching models to 'reason' rather than to 'explain an already-known answer.'

The '3D-aware' and 'depth-informed' claims rest on monocular pseudo-depth (DepthAnythingV2) and pseudo-3D ordinal depths, and the 3D grounding benchmark (Table 4) is evaluated against these same pseudo-GT depths. Training on pseudo-depth and evaluating against pseudo-depth is circular; no true 3D/depth ground truth is used, so the headline '3D grounding' claim is not substantiated.

Evaluation relies on GPT-based scalar grading, while the data itself is generated by the GPT-4.1 family. This creates a plausible self-consistency bias (models distilled to mimic GPT outputs are favored by a GPT judge), and no large-scale calibration of the judge against human judgments is provided (the human study is only 20 items/method).

The headline gains are modest and partly inconsistent with the claims: the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B already scores 0.770 on the Visual-CoT average vs. 0.807 for VisReason-Pro-7B (+3.7 pts), while MME degrades (0.808 -> 0.777) and remains well below InternVL-2.5-8B (0.848). Calling these 'substantial improvements' overstates the evidence.

The comparison to baselines on the self-designed RoI/3D benchmark (Tables 3-4) is asymmetric: baselines are not trained for the multi-round zoom interface, and VisReason-Pro is trained with ADJUSTROI forcing predicted boxes to always cover the GT box. This likely inflates the reported IoU@0.5 (0.34) relative to what genuine localization ability would produce, and the metric may partly reward learned box inflation.

Novelty is incremental. The work is explicitly built on Visual-CoT and largely re-implements its seed pipeline with added segmentation/depth cues; there is no new algorithmic idea, and no controlled ablation isolating the value of the proposed dataset versus the original Visual-CoT under an identical base model and training recipe.

Absolute numbers for the new capabilities are low (IoU@0.5 = 0.34, grounded ratio = 0.276, BBox IoU = 0.278), which weakens the practical significance of the 'spatially grounded' contribution even if relatively better than baselines.

Dataset quality is not independently verified: the auto-generated rationales/boxes are not human-checked at scale, and there is no reported inter-annotator agreement, no error analysis of the GPT-generated chains, and no discussion of licensing/consent for the aggregated source datasets.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on closed GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini for data generation and on GPT-based grading; the paper does not clearly state whether the dataset, benchmark, and generation code will be released or under what terms.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: VisReason (489K) and VisReason-Pro (165K) provide large-scale, multi-round, RoI-grounded visual CoT supervision across four diverse domains, addressing a genuine gap in process-level visual reasoning data.

Comprehensive experimental validation: the paper reports SOTA comparisons on the Visual-CoT benchmark (0.802 avg vs 0.770 baseline), ablation studies isolating dataset variants and the zoom-in strategy, a second-backbone transfer (InternVL-2.5-8B), a 30-participant human study, and a stratified human audit of 2,200 examples with Wilson confidence intervals.

Careful data-construction pipeline with verification loops: AdjustRoI enforce GT coverage, local-to-global coordinate mapping, consistency checks on bounding boxes, and depth-guided region merging make the annotation process more robust than naive prompting.

Good reproducibility practices: detailed training hyperparameters (Tables 10, 11), algorithms for both pipelines (Algorithms 1, 2), evaluation protocols, and all generation/grading prompts are provided in the supplementary material.

Honest and informative discussion of limitations, including format-induced degradation on Text/Doc tasks, cascading localization errors, pseudo-depth noise, and the trade-offs between SFT and RL for learning cropping policies.
The depth-augmented grounding (ordinal depth from monocular cues) and the explicit RoI supervision are a meaningful step beyond single-step 2D visual CoT resources.
weaknesses: The reasoning traces are generated entirely by proprietary VLMs (GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini), so the 'chain-of-thought' supervision may reflect plausible-sounding rationalizations rather than faithful human-like reasoning; the true quality and diversity of rationales are not verified against human-authored reasoning.

Evaluation relies heavily on a GPT-4o-mini judge; while calibration statistics (r=0.758, QWK=0.819) are reported, the circularity of using LLM-based generation and LLM-based grading weakens the strength of the empirical claims.

Potential training/test overlap: the VisReason training sources (Table 1) include the same datasets used in the Visual-CoT evaluation suite (e.g., Open Images, GQA, VSR), and the reported in-domain gains (e.g., Open Images 0.498→0.805) may partly reflect same-distribution fine-tuning rather than genuinely transferable reasoning; the source-removal ablation in D.3 partially addresses this but undercuts the generalization framing.

The '3D grounding' claim is oversold: supervision is pseudo-depth from monocular estimation, the reported depth-error improvement is marginal (0.266 vs 0.294), and the authors themselves acknowledge it should not be read as metric reconstruction.

Multi-round visual CoT is shown to degrade performance on text/document tasks (Table 3: 0.892 vs 0.920 for Qwen baseline), indicating the proposed paradigm is not uniformly beneficial and may introduce unnecessary overhead on tasks that are already solvable from a global view.

The methodological novelty for a computer-vision venue is modest: the core construction is prompting a strong VLM to produce annotations, then filtering/refining; the primary contribution is scale and format rather than a new algorithm or training objective.

strengths: Targets an important gap: large-scale, process-level, spatially grounded visual chain-of-thought data for MLLMs, rather than only final-answer VQA supervision.

Introduces a large and diverse dataset: 489K examples across four domains, plus the 165K VisReason-Pro subset with depth-informed annotations, segmentation cues, and multi-round ROI-grounded rationales.

The annotation design is well motivated: it supports global-to-local zoom-and-verify reasoning with per-round scene descriptions, ROI boxes, and rationales, going beyond single-step visual CoT resources.

Provides a corresponding evaluation suite for stepwise reasoning, ROI localization, and ordinal-depth grounding, with experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL-2.5-8B showing gains in fine-grained recognition, spatial relation reasoning, and ROI localization.
Includes useful reproducibility and validation details: prompts, algorithms, hyperparameters, human audit of annotation quality, GPT-judge calibration, and explicit limitations discussion.
The human study and ablations support the claim that multi-round spatial supervision and adaptive zoom-in contribute to improved grounded reasoning performance.
weaknesses: The dataset generation and automatic evaluation depend heavily on proprietary GPT models (e.g., GPT-4.1-Nano/Mini for annotation, GPT-4o-mini as judge), which limits exact reproducibility and may introduce model-version/API-dependent bias and evaluation drift.

Human audit shows rationale quality is only moderate: overall rationale necessity and faithfulness are around 86.5%, with Text/Doc rationale faithfulness around 72%, so the claim of high-quality reasoning traces is only partially supported.

Training and evaluation are largely in-domain: the dataset is derived from Visual-CoT source datasets and evaluated heavily on the same source benchmark families. Gains may partly reflect domain-specific supervision, and the source-removal ablation indicates strong reliance on domain-relevant training data.

External generalization is not convincingly demonstrated: on MME and V*, the model is roughly on par with or slightly below the base model, and the format-mismatch explanation does not fully rule out limited transferability to broader visual reasoning benchmarks.

Depth supervision relies on pseudo-depth from a monocular estimator and is acknowledged as noisy; the depth-based QA/metrics therefore provide ordinal cues rather than reliable 3D grounding, which weakens the depth-aware spatial reasoning claim.

The adaptive zoom-and-verify pipeline increases inference cost/latency, but the paper does not quantify this trade-off or compare it systematically against non-iterative equally sized training baselines.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: visual chain-of-thought reasoning and spatially grounded process supervision for MLLMs, where existing resources are limited.
It introduces a large-scale dataset (489K examples; VisReason-Pro 165K) spanning four domains, with multi-round RoI-grounded rationales and depth/segmentation cues.
The data-generation pipeline, evaluation suite, and training/inference protocol are described in detail, including prompts, algorithms, and supplementary material, supporting reproducibility.

The empirical study includes multiple backbones, external benchmarks, ablations, human evaluation, and a human-audited calibration of the GPT judge, showing gains on fine-grained and spatial reasoning and RoI localization.
The authors discuss limitations such as depth noise, cascading localization errors, and format-dependent evaluation mismatch, which is useful context.
weaknesses: The annotations, including the reasoning chains, are generated by GPT-4.1 models rather than human-written; human audit indicates nontrivial rates of unfaithful or unnecessary rationales (86.5%), leaving step-level reasoning quality unverified and risking post-hoc rationalization.

Potential data contamination: VisReason is derived from the Visual-CoT dataset, and evaluation also follows Visual-CoT benchmark. It is unclear whether training and test splits are disjoint; if not, comparisons and generalization claims are invalid.

Experimental comparisons are not sufficiently controlled: main results compare their fine-tuned models against zero-shot/frozen MLLMs, without fine-tuning the same base model on original/alternative supervision under identical compute, so gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed dataset.

Automatic evaluation relies on GPT-4o-mini as judge rather than exact accuracy; format-sensitive prompts can reward verbose CoT or penalize baselines, and the reported gains are uneven (Doc/Text performance drops; InternVL transfer only +0.001 overall).

Depth/3D supervision is based on noisy monocular pseudo-depth and segmentation, not ground-truth geometry; the depth-related metrics show only small improvements, and no convincing evidence demonstrates that models learn true ordinal-depth reasoning.

RoI localization evaluation may be biased: training targets are post-adjusted to contain ground-truth boxes, and baselines are prompted without grounding-specific fine-tuning, making the RoI comparisons uneven.

The core technical contribution is limited: the method is essentially GPT-based annotation plus standard supervised fine-tuning with LoRA; no new architecture, objective, or inference algorithm is introduced beyond serializing boxes and rationales.

The human study is small (20 items/method, 30 raters) and does not report expert qualifications, annotator agreement, or statistical tests; it does not establish that the generated rationales are faithful or that the model is more interpretable.

Dataset documentation is incomplete for a dataset/benchmark contribution: licensing, consent, source-data terms, annotation cost, inter-annotator agreement, and maintenance plan are not adequately discussed; societal impact and bias are not addressed.

There are reproducibility concerns: single-run results, no error bars/confidence intervals on main metrics, and some training details (e.g., dynamic cropping, answer extraction) may be sensitive to implementation choices.
